items.title: Update benchmark numbers to reflect the serde-saphyr backend
items.body:
The README and docs still quoted benchmark numbers from before the serde-saphyr swap (#36), which overstated load performance.

Re-ran `benchmarks/bench.py` and `benchmarks/bench_formats.py` on a release build (confirmed stable across runs) and updated `README.md` + `docs/performance.md`:

- **vcrpy comparison (1000 interactions):** the old table claimed load `13.53 ms` / `4.4x`. Actual is ~`35 ms` / `2.7x`. Save is `~6.5 ms` / `11.8x` (was `7.58 ms` / `6.0x`), match `~1.4x`. Headline changed from "3-6x faster" to the honest "2-3x on load and 7-12x on save."
- **TOML vs YAML:** "~2x faster load" is now ~2.8x; added the caveat that TOML saves are slower (it was implied but not stated). Sizes unchanged (768/675 KB).
- Added a note that absolute timings are machine-dependent (ratios are the portable part) and that load speedup varies with cassette shape - the many-tiny-interactions synthetic is the parser's worst case, while large-body cassettes (LLM/SSE) load proportionally faster.

The direction of the correction is honest: serde-saphyr traded some raw parse speed on this synthetic shape for security guarantees, active maintenance, and faster loads on large-body cassettes (measured 2.5x faster than the old backend on the pydantic-ai corpus). Docs-only; no code change.

## Summary                                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                            
  This PR updates the precise prefix cache routing guide for SGLang with significantly improved benchmark results and includes the configuration tuning that enabled these gains.                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                            
 By tuning SGLang's memory allocation ( --mem-fraction-static=0.9 ), we unlocked drastically better performance under high load, maintaining stable, sub-second TTFT (Time to First Token) even at peak request rates where it previously degraded. Prior to this change, the default usage was coming out to be around 0.82 percent.                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                            
  ## Key Changes                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                            
  ### 1. SGLang Configuration Tune                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                
  • Added  --mem-fraction-static=0.9  to patch-sglang.yaml. This optimizes GPU memory utilization for the KV cache, which is critical for sustaining high prefix-matching performance under concurrency.      
                                                                                                                                                                                                            
  ### 2. Updated Benchmark Results (README.md)                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                            
  • Clarified Setup: Noted that the benchmark runs on 16× H100 GPUs across 8 model servers (TP=2).                                                                                                          
  • Added Summary Table: Introduced a high-level comparison table across the full ladder (rates 3 to 60) highlighting the massive gains of  llm-d Precise  over the standard Kubernetes round-robin         
  baseline:                                                                                                                                                                                                 
      • Output Throughput: +110.2% (~2x increase).                                                                                                                                                          
      • Mean TTFT: -99.33% (reduced from ~70s to 466ms).                                                                                                                                                    
      • p90 TTFT: -99.57% (reduced from ~157s to 672ms).                                                                                                                                                    
  • Updated Detailed Ladder: Refreshed the per-rate breakdown table with the new run data and extended the test ladder up to rate 60 (previously capped at 52).                                             
      • Note on improvement: Previously, at rate 52,  llm-d  mean TTFT had risen to ~20 seconds. With the static memory fraction patch, mean TTFT at rate 52 is now 0.328 seconds, and remains stable at 0.

items.title: refactor: extract c2py_ptr_info from Py_buffer
items.body:
## Summary

Introduces `c2py_ptr_info` (a simplified buffer metadata struct) and
`c2py_buf_pin` (a wrapper holding the opaque `Py_buffer` and its
acquired flag).  Generated wrappers now operate on `c2py_ptr_info`
everywhere; `Py_buffer` access is isolated to `c2py_pin_buffer` /
`c2py_unpin_buffer`.

This is a **pure structural refactor** with no behavioral change — all
96 tests pass identically.

## Why

The current generated code talks directly to `Py_buffer` fields
(`buf_foo->buf`, `buf_foo->ndim`, etc.).  This makes it impossible
to swap in alternative buffer acquisition backends (numpy ndarray
struct cast, DLPack capsule extraction) without touching every
reference in the generated wrapper.

By introducing a common `c2py_ptr_info` struct with fields
`ptr`, `ndim`, `len`, `itemsize`, `format`, `shape`,
`strides`, the generated code operates on a uniform interface.
The `pin`/`unpin` pair hides the acquisition mechanism.  Future
PRs can add `c2py_pin_ndarray()` or `c2py_pin_dlpack()` that
fill the same struct without any wrapper changes.

## Changes

- **`c2py_runtime.h`**: Add `c2py_ptr_info`, `c2py_buf_pin`,
  `c2py_pin_buffer()`, `c2py_unpin_buffer()`
- **`generator.py`**: Declare `pin` + `info` instead of
  `Py_buffer` + `acq` flag; call `c2py_pin_buffer`/`unpin`
  instead of `acquire`/`release`; update `_impl` signatures and
  restrict/contiguity checks
- **`parser.py`**: Var prefix `buf_` -> `info_`, Attr `.ptr` ->
  `->ptr`
- **`invariant_checker.py`**: Update regexes for new struct types
  and function names
- **`xfrm_wrapper.c`**: Regenerated
- **`benchmarks/`**: Updated numbers

## Benchmark impact

Tiny buffer ops show the overhead of unpacking `Py_buffer` into
`c2py_ptr_info` (7 field copies):

| Test | Before | After | Delta |
|------|--------|-------|-------|
| vnorm bare tiny | 122ns | 164ns | +42ns |
| vnorm checks | 128ns | 149ns | +21ns |
| getitem numpy | 126ns | 134ns | +8ns |
| getitem array | 93ns | 96ns | +3ns |
| noargs | 24.5ns | 24.5ns | -- |

Large vnorm throughput is unchanged (10.6ms, ~12.7 GB/s).

This cost reverses in Phase 2 when the ndarray struct-cast fast-path
fills `c2py_ptr_info` directly, skipping `PyObject_GetBuffer`
entirely.

## Test results

96/96 tests pass on Python 3.12:
- 18 uniform tests
- 10 peer review tests (alias + contiguity)
- 31 regression tests
- 7 error path refcount tests
- 12 leak stress tests
- 10 lifecycle tests

items.title: Add Brotli compression, auth helpers, and streaming response bodies
items.body:
## Summary

This PR adds Brotli compression support, HTTP authentication helpers (Basic and Bearer), and refactors the HTTP response model to always stream bodies over the live connection rather than buffering them. It also introduces read timeouts, OS-native TLS certificate verification, and several quality-of-life improvements to the HTTP client.

## Key Changes

**Compression:**
- Add `Compression::Brotli` variant (HTTP `Content-Encoding: br`) with full codec support
- Implement Brotli encode/decode via the `brotli` crate (optional feature, on by default)
- Update `MimeType` to include `Brotli` and add `Compression::mime()` to map codecs to their MIME types
- Surface compression metadata in bindings: `content_encoding()`, `compression()`, `mime_type()`, and `media_type()` (layered type stack)

**HTTP Authentication:**
- Add `with_basic_auth(username, password)` and `with_bearer_auth(token)` to both `HttpRequest` and `HttpSession`
- Implement dependency-free Base64 encoder in new `auth.rs` module for HTTP Basic credentials
- Per-request auth overrides session-level auth (no duplicate headers)

**Response Streaming & Connection Management:**
- Refactor `HttpSession::send()` signature: remove `keep_alive` and `stream` parameters; **all sends now stream** the response body over the live connection
- Add `keep_alive` TTL to `HttpRequest` (default 5 minutes, `Duration::ZERO` disables pooling)
- Introduce `DEFAULT_READ_TIMEOUT` (2 minutes) with `HttpSession::with_read_timeout()` to bound stalled servers
- Configure `ureq` agent with `timeout_recv_response` and `timeout_recv_body` to surface timeouts instead of hanging
- Add `HttpResponse::body_mut()` to access the raw undecoded stream in place
- Add `HttpResponse::read_all()` to drain the body and capture `received_at` timestamp

**TLS & Certificate Verification:**
- Switch default TLS to **OS-native certificate store** (Windows SChannel, macOS Security, Linux system bundle) via `ureq::tls::RootCerts::PlatformVerifier`
- Keep custom CA cert support via `with_ca_cert()` (overrides the default store when non-empty)

**Session Management:**
- Add `HttpSession::copy()` to create an independent session with the same configuration and a snapshot of cookies, but a fresh connection pool
- Add `HttpHeaders::copy()` for independent header set copies

**Bindings:**
- Node.js: Update `RequestTask` to use new `send()` signature; drain body via `read_all()` to capture `received_at`
- Python: Add `content_encoding()`, `mime_type()`, `media_type()`, `compression()`, and `io` (BytesIO handle) accessors to `HttpResponse`; add `json()` method; update `HttpSession` to accept `basic_auth` and `bearer_auth` parameters
- Both: Surface Brotli in compression tests

**Documentation & Tests:**
- Update `CLAUDE.md` to document Brotli and the new auth/streaming model
- Add comprehensive tests for Basic/Bearer auth (per-request and per-session)
- Add test for Brotli decompression
- Rename `buffered_send_drains_the_body_and_releases_the_connection` to `streamed_send_holds_the_connection_until_the_body_drains` to reflect the new always-streaming model
- Update benchmark numbers and add Brotli compression benchmarks
- Update HTTP documentation with examples of the new auth and media-type APIs

## Implementation Details

- The `keep_alive` TTL is now a `Duration` field on `HttpRequest`, set via `with_keep_alive()` (default `DEFAULT_KEEP_ALIVE = 5 minutes`)
- `HttpSession::send()` now takes only `(request, raise_error)` — the connection is held until the body is drained or the response is dropped
- Read timeouts

items.title: #256 — il dizionario mercati ricompilava se stesso a ogni messaggio (108 ms → 7,6 ms)
items.body:
Chiude il **punto 1** di #256. Il punto 2 (tetto per profilo) resta aperto lì: è un limite noto e misurato, senza urgenza.

## Il difetto

`_phrase_in_text` costruisce il regex a confini di token dalla frase e lo passa a `re.search` come **stringa**:

```python
return re.search(r"(?<[\w/-])(?<!\d[.,])" + re.escape(p) + r"(?[\w/-])(?[.,]\d)",
                 text_norm) is not None
```

Il pattern dipende **solo** dalla frase, ma veniva ricostruito e ricompilato a ogni chiamata — cioè **una volta per voce, per messaggio**. Il modulo `re` tiene una cache interna di ~512 pattern: finché il dizionario ci sta sotto non si vede nulla, appena la supera **ogni messaggio ricompila l'intero dizionario**.

Misurato sul percorso live (`resolve_market`, media su 20 messaggi):

| frasi mappate | prima | dopo |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 100 | 0,73 ms | 0,61 ms |
| 400 | 2,98 ms | 2,51 ms |
| 600 | **54,04 ms** | 3,86 ms |
| 1200 | 108,42 ms | 7,62 ms |

Il dirupo cade esattamente dove ci si aspetta. **Il tetto introdotto dalla #255 non c'entra**: protegge solo la diagnostica allo START. Il runtime non ha tetto e non può averne uno — non si può rifiutare di risolvere un mercato perché il dizionario è grande.

Non è perdita di segnali né scommessa sbagliata: è latenza sul percorso che scrive il CSV.

## La patch

Una `lru_cache` di modulo indicizzata sulla frase **normalizzata**: «GG», «gg» e «  gg  » sono la stessa frase per il matching, quindi la stessa voce di cache — indicizzare sul grezzo moltiplicherebbe le voci e riaprirebbe il thrashing che la cache chiude.

Il `maxsize` è deliberato, non decorativo: le frasi arrivano dal config dell'utente, e una cache illimitata su input utente è una perdita di memoria lenta. Oltre il tetto si sfrattano le voci meno usate e si torna a ricompilare quelle — come prima della patch, senza mai sbagliare risposta.

## Il rischio non era la prestazione, era il matching

`_phrase_in_text` sta sul **percorso soldi**: un confine di token sbagliato qui è un mercato sbagliato, cioè la scommessa sbagliata (P1 già tracciato in `tests/safety/test_money_path_p1_bughunt.py`). Quindi i test non verificano solo che la cache esista, ma che **attraverso la cache il confronto sia identico**.

**Provato per sabotaggio.** Togliendo il lookbehind sul separatore decimale vanno rossi **8 test** — 4 nel file nuovo e 4 nel money-path:

```
FAILED ..._il_matching_attraverso_la_cache_e_identico[over 2-over 2.5-False]
FAILED ..._il_matching_attraverso_la_cache_e_identico[5 ht-1,5 ht-False]
FAILED ..._il_matching_attraverso_la_cache_e_identico[5-2,5-False]
FAILED test_money_path_p1_bughunt.py::test_frase_intera_non_matcha_linea_decimale_diversa
FAILED test_money_path_p1_bughunt.py::test_phrase_in_text_esclude_separatore_decimale
FAILED test_money_path_p1_bughunt.py::test_separatore_come_punteggiatura_finale_resta_confine
FAILED test_money_path_p1_bughunt.py::test_confine_decimale_sinistro_virgola_e_punto
```

## Test — fail-first, verificato rosso

I test contano le **compilazioni reali** (`re._compiler.compile`, invocato solo sui cache miss) invece dei millisecondi: un'asserzione a cronometro è flaky su un runner condiviso e misura la cosa sbagliata — il punto non è «è veloce», è «non ricompila».

Sul codice pre-patch:

```
AssertionError: 3018 compilazioni per 5 messaggi con 600 frasi: il dizionario
                viene ricompilato a ogni messaggio
assert 3018 <= (600 + 50)
```

3018 = 5 × ~600, esattamente il difetto.

| Test | Cosa blocca |
|---|---|
| `..._non_si_ricompilano_a_ogni_messaggio` | il difetto della issue, contato |
| `..._lo_stesso_messaggio_ripetuto_non_compila_piu_nulla` | il regime reale: dopo il warm-up le compilazioni sono **zero**, non «poche» |
| `..._la_cache_e_indicizzata_sulla_frase_NORMALIZZATA` | 4 varianti di case/spazi → **1** voce di cache |
| `..._il_matching_attraverso_la_cache_e_identico` ×15 | l'invariante P1 del percorso soldi |
| `..._la_cache_e_limitata_e_non_cresce_senza_fine` | `maxsize` presente, e risposte corrette anche oltre il tetto |

## L'effetto collaterale che non nascondo

La patch rende **false** le misure che giustificavano il tetto della #255: `800 voci = 54 s` sono ora **4,53 s**. Erano scritte in **quattro punti** — due commenti, un docstring di test, il design doc — e sono state corrette tutte. Lasciarle sarebbe stato lo stesso difetto inseguito per tutta la #253 e la #255: un testo che dice altro da ciò che il codice fa.

**Il tetto resta a 300.** Il costo è ancora quadratico e 1200 voci costano 9 s allo START. È oggi più conservativo del necessario, e l'ho scritto nel codice invece di alzarlo di nascosto: alzarlo è una decisione a sé, con la sua misura.

## Sicurezza

- **CSV / Betfair:** nessuna modifica al contratto. Il confronto è identico — provato per sabotaggio.
- **Telegram / `chat_id` / config:** non toccati.
- **Aree dichiarate sane:** non toccate.
- **Fratelli cercati e misurati** (regola 2): 4 siti costruiscono un regex da una variabile. `_has_ref_token` gira **una volta per segnale pending** e il design è one-signal-at-a-time → nessun moltiplicatore; `diagnostics.py:169` non è hot path; `custom_pipeline.py:197` ha pochi valori distinti. Solo `_phrase_in_text` ha il moltiplicatore N-per-messaggio, quindi solo lì serve la cache.

## Verifica

`5118 passed, 1 skipped`. `ruff`: **69 → 69** (invariato). `python -m py_compile main.py`: OK.

items.body:
## Summary

This PR substantially rewrites the README to emphasize correctness as the primary design goal, adds three new benchmark suites to the codebase, and refactors the `MemoryPool` allocator to eliminate hot-path overhead while properly accounting for overflow.

## Key Changes

**Documentation & Philosophy**
- Reframe the project from "fastest" to "correct first, measured honestly second"
- Add dedicated "Correctness" section documenting four test suites: unit tests, randomized differential testing against a reference model, LOBSTER real-market-data reconciliation, and allocator lifetime testing
- Expand "Real Market-Data Reconciliation (LOBSTER)" section with detailed event mapping, seeding logic for pre-window liquidity, and strict vs. recover reconciliation modes
- Rewrite "Performance" section with honest caveats about timer resolution, machine context, and tail latency on shared VMs
- Update all benchmark numbers to reflect actual measured values on Ubuntu 24.04 with `std::chrono::steady_clock`
- Add timer overhead disclosure (22 ns) and explain how it's included/excluded from reported figures

**Benchmark Suite Additions** (`benchmarks/benchmark_latency.cpp`)
- `bench_allocator()`: A/B test `MemoryPool<Order>` vs. global `new`/`delete` on identical steady-state churn (hold 20k live orders, repeatedly release and allocate replacements). Shows ~26 ns savings at p50, ~256 ns at p99.9.
- `bench_trade_handler()`: Measure the cost of the `std::function` trade-reporting hook via identical single-fill crossing inserts with handler unset vs. set. Quantifies the ~2 ns/fill dispatch overhead.
- Both benchmarks include guards against invalid comparisons (pool overflow, missing fills).

**MemoryPool Refactoring** (`include/MemoryPool.hpp`)
- Remove `stderr` logging from `allocate()` hot path (was a flushed, locked syscall per overflow)
- Add sticky `has_overflowed_` flag to guard the heap-pointer lookup in `deallocate()`, eliminating the hash probe on every release for pools that stay within capacity
- Add `overflow_total()` to track cumulative overflow count (distinct from live count)
- Add `has_overflowed()` query for out-of-band reporting
- Update `deallocate()` to only consult `heap_allocated` set if the pool has ever overflowed

**MemoryPool Test Expansion** (`tests/test_memorypool.cpp`)
- Add overflow path test: drive a tiny 4-slot pool past capacity, interleave pooled and heap releases in random order, verify each pointer routes correctly and reused slots are genuinely reusable
- Validates the fast-path guard: a heap pointer mistaken for pooled would be placement-destroyed and filed onto the free list, causing heap corruption — the test catches this under AddressSanitizer

**OrderBook Documentation** (`include/OrderBook.hpp`)
- Add comment explaining the ~2 ns/fill cost of `std::function` dispatch and why templating on handler type is deliberately not done (would make engine header-only and couple its type to its observer)

## Notable Implementation Details

- The `has_overflowed_` flag is sticky (never reset) so the reasoning about deallocate's fast path stays trivially correct: false means no heap pointer has ever been handed out, therefore this pointer must be pooled.
- Overflow is recorded but not logged from the hot path; the caller can report it out of band via `overflow_total()` at a point of its own choosing.
- All benchmark figures now include explicit machine context (Ubuntu 24.04, Intel Xeon @ 2.80 GHz, GCC 13.3.0) and timer overhead (22 ns), with caveats about tail latency on shared VMs.
- The LOBSTER reconciliation section now documents the seeding strategy for pre-window liquidity and the two reconciliation modes (strict horizon vs. recover-and-count).

items.title: feat(codegen): XMM register direct RHS for FP binops (ms178-1.patch v3)
items.body:
## Summary

Apply the latest [ms178-1.patch](https://github.com/ms178/archpkgbuilds/blob/main/toolchain-experimental/claudes-c-compiler/ms178-1.patch) (100 lines) from the archpkgbuilds repo against current HEAD.

## What's in the patch

The upstream patch contains three hunks:

| File | Change | Status in main |
|---|---|---|
| `src/backend/x86/codegen/float_ops.rs` | RHS XMM register direct for FP binops | **New — applied in this PR** |
| `src/backend/x86/codegen/memory.rs` | AVX2 vmovdqu 32B memcpy | Already present (PR #16, superset) |
| `tests/regression/fp_domain_crossing.c` | FP domain crossing regression test | Already present (PR #16, superset) |

## The actual delta

**`float_ops.rs` (+34 lines):** In `emit_float_binop_impl`, the `Operand::Value(v)` arm for the RHS now checks `reg_assignments` first. When the value is already in an XMM register (xmm3–xmm7, assigned by the register allocator), the FP binop operates directly (e.g. `addsd %xmm5, %xmm0`) instead of detouring through GPR scratch (`movq %xmm5, %rcx; movq %rcx, %xmm1; addsd %xmm1, %xmm0`). This saves 2–3 instructions per FP chain operation.

Result storage handles three dest cases:
- **Stack slot**: `movsd %xmm0, slot` (direct)
- **XMM register dest**: xmm-to-xmm move
- **GPR / unassigned**: `movd`/`movq` through eax/rax + `store_rax_to`

Safe because xmm3–xmm7 are never clobbered by codegen scratch (xmm0/xmm1 are the only scratch XMM registers).

## Benchmark impact (v3 vs v2 baseline, i7-14700KF, 7 rounds)

| Benchmark | v2 Ratio | v3 Ratio | Improvement |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **nbody** | 8.21× | **5.23×** | **-36%** |
| **spectral_norm** | 12.67× | **9.57×** | **-26%** |
| **mandelbrot** | 4.77× | **4.23×** | **-11%** |
| **arith_loop** | 1.11× | **1.04×** | **-7%** |
| Geomean | 1.20× | **1.16×** | — |

## Remaining gap

The primary bottleneck is **no auto-vectorization**. GCC uses AVX2 4-wide double ops (`vdivpd`, `vmulpd`, `vaddsd` with ymm registers) for FP reductions. LCCC is fully scalar. This accounts for spectral_norm (9.57×), nbody (5.23×), and mandelbrot (4.23×).

## Patch applicability

- Applied with **zero fuzz** against HEAD (`0d0d3ce`)
- No workflow file changes (patch doesn't include any)
- memory.rs and fp_domain_crossing.c hunks already present via PR #16
